Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): okay everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off in a minute. Quick intros?
[00:10] Ayesha (Cyclone): hi, I'm Ayesha, head of ML at Cyclone Security, focused on productionizing our conversational assistant for SOC workflows.
[00:18] Tom (Cyclone): Tom, CTO--we're making sure the infra can meet 99.9 SLA.
[00:23] Ravi (Cyclone): Ravi, platform, I'll be running the benchmark work.
[00:27] Sofia: great, Devon and Maya from our side, Devon will walk the Optimize console sims and Maya will cover recommended configs for KV prefetch and TTL.
[00:35] Devon (Redwood): cool, jumping in. So today we'll show an Optimize walkthrough: two things, batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations, and a cost sim you can run with your session histogram. We'll start with the console, then the cost spreadsheet.
[00:50] [00:50] Devon: first, quick question—what are your typical session lengths and how bursty is traffic?
[00:56] Ayesha: most sessions are short, like three to five turns, but we have investigation flows that are long—up to 120 tokens per turn and sessions up to 20 turns. It's spiky during incident windows.
[01:10] Devon: perfect, that's the pattern Optimize was built for—prefetch helps a lot for multi-turn. Also curious on latency budget?
[01:17] Tom: 150 to 200 ms p50, 350 ms p95 is our internal target.
[01:23] Sofia: okay notes on latency and tail—good. I'll also call out security constraints?
[01:27] Lena: we require customer-managed keys and audit logs, and prefer private or VPC deployments for sensitive logs. SOC 2 is a hard ask.
[01:35] Maya (Redwood): totally understood. We have private deployment options; we'll share SOC2 docs and network diagrams after this call.
[01:41] Devon: jumping into the console—loading optimize runbook... (screen share)
[01:46] [02:02] Devon: this is the cost-sim panel. On the left you can paste your session histogram; we'll default with a demo histogram for now. You can toggle hosted versus dedicated and choose KV-prefetch strategy: none, prefix-only, full-kv.
[02:18] Ravi: what's the difference between prefix-only and full-kv in practice?
[02:22] Devon: good question. Prefix-only caches the transformer key/values for the initial token prefixes—good for short repeated prompts. Full-KV tries to store the entire context KV for a session and reuse it across requests—more memory but higher hit rate for long dialogs. If your sessions often revisit the same context, full-KV wins.
[02:40] Ayesha: and TTL? we don't want stale secrets in cache.
[02:44] Maya: TTL is configurable per model/policy. We suggest conservative TTL for security-sensitive contexts—like 5–15 minutes with explicit invalidation on logout. For private deployments we can tie TTL to your cache invalidation hooks.
[02:57] [03:15] Devon: next, batching. On this chart you can set concurrency and target latency SLO; Optimize will recommend micro-batch sizes and a continuous batching policy. For example, at 200ms target we'll suggest smaller batch sizes to keep p95 latency in budget.
[03:31] Tom: can you show the cost delta?
[03:34] Devon: yep. Switching the sim to your histogram—okay I'm dropping in a 80/15/5 distribution (short/medium/long). With no prefetch and naive batching, the cost per 1M tokens is X (placeholder), with prefix-only it drops about 18%, with full-KV it drops ~36% but memory footprint grows.
[03:52] Sofia: note that those percentages are demo numbers; we'll run them with your real histogram in the sheet.
[03:58] Ravi: are those numbers factoring in quantization or model variant fallback?
[04:03] Devon: in this sim it's model-variant-aware: we show options to route older sessions to quantized 4-bit variants for cost savings. Optimize also recommends when to roll the 4-bit for a given quality loss budget.
[04:15] [04:30] Ayesha: hmm, we have strict quality needs for certain flows. How do you guard against hallucination regressions when switching quantized models?
[04:36] Maya: good point—Optimize ties to your eval sets. You can pin prompts and thresholds: if quality drops beyond X we auto-fallback to higher fidelity model. We surface eval deltas per rollout.
[04:47] Ravi: can we simulate peak incident traffic—like 5x baseline for 30 minutes?
[04:52] Devon: yes, the sim can run burst scenarios and will propose burst capacity options. In Hosted we offer burst pools; in Dedicated you can pre-reserve capacity or set autoscale policies.
[05:05] [05:20] Tom: on private deployment, how different is the KV implementation? We worry about data exfil.
[05:25] Maya: same design but you control the cache backend. For VPC/on-prem we support Redis or in-process cache behind your KMS; keys never leave your network per config. We can also add HSM support for key wrapping.
[05:39] Lena: perfect, send the docs.
[05:42] Devon: switching to a concrete sim—I'm going to paste a synthetic session histogram that mimics what you described. (typing) You can see the recommended TTL and memory footprint on the right.
[05:55] [06:10] Devon: with 10k concurrent sessions and average 6 turns, prefix-only gives a 22% token cost reduction and keeps memory under our 3GB per-GPU threshold. Full-KV shows 48% token cost reduction but memory jumps to 12GB per-GPU which would require a different instance type.
[06:28] Ravi: that memory jump is the blocker for our current infra. What about partial prefetch—evict older turns, keep last N turns?
[06:36] Devon: yes, Optimize supports sliding-window KV: keep last K turns or last N tokens. That's often the best hybrid—80% of savings with only 30% of the memory penalty.
[06:45] Ayesha: any impact on cold start latency?
[06:48] Devon: small—when session first arrives there's a prefetch step that adds a few ms, but we overlap network fetch with compute where possible. For p50 targets you won't notice, p95 maybe +10–20ms depending on backend.
[06:59] [07:20] Tom: can you show the console's batch heatmap?
[07:24] Devon: sure—here's the heatmap. It suggests batching windows of 8–16ms at your observed concurrency to achieve ideal GPU occupancy. We also expose continuous batching thresholds so you don't have to pick a fixed batch size.
[07:38] Ravi: do you provide logs for per-token cost attribution?
[07:41] Maya: yes, Console exposes per-token cost, per-route breakdowns, and traces down to token group. That helped one customer find a rogue prompt that was doubling token usage.
[07:52] [08:05] Ayesha: what about compute fallback—if one region is saturated, how do you route?
[08:09] Devon: Optimize's routing layer will failover to compatible model variants or other regions based on policy. You can set policy to prefer lower-cost region with slightly higher latency or keep strict latency and pay up for warm capacity.
[08:22] Tom: I'm worried about procurement complexity: hosted invoices vs dedicated-level contracts.
[08:27] Sofia: we typically run a pilot on hosted with dedicated pricing blended for predictability, then move to Dedicated or Private for enterprise contracts. We'll send standard SOW and sample pricing templates.
[08:39] [09:00] Devon: a quick demo of adjusting the prefetch policy—I'm toggling sliding window to last-3-turns and reducing TTL to 7 minutes. See memory estimate drop and cost delta.
[09:12] Ravi: excellent. Can that be controlled per-route? We have some routes that are low-sensitivity and others that are compliance-critical.
[09:18] Devon: yes, per-route policies are supported. You can attach a security label and different TTL and cache scopes.
[09:26] [09:40] Ayesha: what about traceability—if we need to audit who accessed which cached KV?
[09:43] Maya: audit logs include cache access events and invalidation events with token-level metadata; for private you can push logs to your SIEM.
[09:50] Tom: does that affect performance?
[09:53] Devon: minimal; logs are emitted asynchronously and sampled at configurable rates.
[09:58] [10:15] (20m mark) Sofia: let's talk about next steps—Pilot scope?
[10:20] Tom: pilot to validate p95 latency and cost delta on two critical flows. 1 week run with 1000 concurrent sessions in a staged environment.
[10:29] Ayesha: we will share the actual session histogram and a small eval set for regression checks.
[10:33] Sofia: awesome. Devon, Maya—action items?
[10:36] Devon: I'll run the cost sim with their real histogram and post the spreadsheet. Also will run a burst test scenario for 5x.
[10:42] Maya: I'll share Optimize runbook and a recommended TTL matrix for sensitivity tiers.
[10:47] (brief side conversation)
[10:52] Ravi: question—what's the typical savings customers see moving from no-cache to sliding-window?
[10:56] Devon: depends on dialog shape; for security assistants like yours we usually see 25–40% token savings and 20–35% cost savings after accounting for memory+instance delta. But again it hinges on how much context repeats.
[11:10] Ayesha: and if we keep everything on private, is the economics worse?
[11:14] Sofia: private has a higher fixed platform fee but gives you control and can be cheaper at scale when paired with dedicated GPU pools—we'll model both.
[11:23] [11:40] Lena: small compliance question—do cached KVs persist across deploys? We need to rotate keys and clear caches on deploy.
[11:46] Maya: we support cache invalidation hooks triggered by CI/CD events; also automatic invalidation on key rotation. We'll add that to the runbook.
[11:56] Devon: quick demo: toggling quantized fallback for a route. If the eval delta >2% we auto-fallback. You can set that threshold.
[12:06] Ravi: can the console show simulated hallucination metrics?
[12:09] Maya: post- rollout you can run synthetic evals; the dashboard will show token-level diffs and hallucination counts from your eval set.
[12:18] [12:35] (crosstalk) Tom: Okay, this is helpful.
[12:38] Sofia: I'll summarize the follow-ups and send the sheet + SOC2 + network diagram.
[12:44] Ayesha: thanks, we want to start the pilot next Monday ideally.
[12:48] Sofia: noted—we'll aim to have the sim and runbook in your hands by Friday.
[12:53] [13:10] (wrap)
[13:12] Sofia: anything else?
[13:15] Tom: no, thanks.
[13:17] Ravi: no, thanks.
[13:20] (meeting ends)
